items.title: Show HN: Open-Sourced Code Mode to Cut ~60% of My Rust Agent's Token Burn
items.summary: For those who are tracking, Anthropic released an announcement last week about their experimental code mode for Claude Code, claiming some bonkers token savings when it comes to tool calls (95% on some workloads(1)). I haven't benchmarked it myself, but independent studies come in somewhere closer to 60~70% savings (2), but I digress. TLDR; I built an open-source version for the community. Context: I'm writing an AI RPG engine called Spookery, and I immediately wanted to try this technique for myself when I heard of it. Agent deployment is currently dominated by token costs, especially during tool calling (single prompt generating tens or hundreds of tool calls). Unfortunately, it looks like the only ones who are doing this seriously are big agentic products like Claude Code and Codex. So, I thought it'd be fun to try it myself and bring it to you all! The idea of Code Mode is simple but powerful. Instead of passing back tool call results back to the LLM one at a time, let the LLM batch calls by letting it write a short script using your tools. Basically taking 30 trips to the grocery store for 30 items and turning it into one trip to the store with a list in-hand. There's a few near-ish open-source options, but they used TypeScript backends, we're a little boilerplate heavy, and I wanted to have something a little faster and Rust friendly for my game engine. Pydantic's Monty seemed a good candidate--their self-reports are around 5x faster on execution and 100x faster on startup (3). I wouldn't take the numbers to the bank, but it's written on a Rust framework and the python backend is entirely built from Rust too. Anyway, I had a couple of days off unexpectedly. So, I went temporarily insane and built a Rust tool to bring code mode to the greater community for free. In enough days to fit on one hand (and just as many hours of sleep), I came up with the implementation linked. I call it Ghost Mode. It's MIT licensed. It's a drop-in for your agent that already makes traditional tool calls. With ~20 lines of setup, you can convert your existing agent to a Code Mode agent. I hope you get something out of this, and maybe I can save you some money. Considering how limiting token economics are right now, I think this could be a game changer for the industry. If there's interest, I can imagine we can build also add some great new features, language compatibility, and other great things. Thanks for reading :) Sources: (1) https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/11/17/anthropic-claude-cod... (2) https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19123 (3) https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/get-started/

items.title: We migrated agent-swarm from SQLite to Postgres
items.story_key: story|title:we migrated agent swarm from sqlite to postgres
items.content_excerpt: The log of 6 days: a swarm writes a PostgreSQL storage engine in one weekend, we copy 24 million rows 3 times, switch production at 01:44, and get the first error at 01:46. On Friday our production swarm stored everything in one SQLite file. 6 days later it ran on PostgreSQL. The plan said before Christmas. We started Agent Swarm on SQLite on purpose. One file is simple to run and easy to deploy. We knew that we would need PostgreSQL if we scaled. Then the scale came. Our own file grew to 87 GB, one long statement could stall the API, and the next steps on our list need a database that several processes can share. KISS paid. SQLite took us this far, and it stays the default. This post is the log of those 6 days. Times are Barcelona time. The mark on each entry says who did the step: Dani or Taras, Dani's swarm, our swarm, a coding session, or CI. We measured the in-process SQLite drivers that run on Bun. Each of them blocks the event loop while a statement runs. The plan from that research was a worker thread for SQLite. We deferred PostgreSQL. Dani runs Agent Swarm at his company and had the same limit. He and Taras agreed on 4 things on a call: A goal, to say: okay, you have all these E2Es. Just switch the connection to Postgres, and ensure that the E2Es pass with both SQLite and Postgres. And that's it. Maybe that's the easiest way to do it. If this is something that we could put under the Christmas tree, I would be super happy. It's doable. It's just a matter of figuring out the good prompt to do that, and then do the last 10%, which is the worst part, which is just ensure that it's okay, okay, okay, and just merge it and that's it. Taras answered with the same model and another style: a brainstorm and a goal prompt . The goal prompt has an objective, 18 numbered decisions, and conditions that say when to stop. it seems you already want to jump into the implementation with a "goal", while mine is trying to be a preliminary research phase before saying "goal: implement direction X, stop when conditions met" 😄 jaja you can run that and correct wht i did, mine was a brainstorm with some bg research The yolo version won. The brainstorm and the goal prompt became the input of the engine build. The research ran first. Dani gave his research prompt to his swarm. The first researcher agent stopped on a usage limit after 21 minutes, and the lead gave the work to a second one. The report came at 18:07 and cost 71 USD. The report checked the 1,495 static SQL stat

items.title: Clawdcursor, a desktop agent that runs UI tasks in the background
items.story_key: story|title:clawdcursor a desktop agent that runs ui tasks in the background
items.content_excerpt: The fallback execution layer: when there's no API, CLI or file edit for the job, your AI uses the screen through clawdcursor. It picks the fastest way into each app: the page itself in browsers, the accessibility tree in desktop apps, text recognition when there's no tree, and screenshots last. After every action it tells your AI whether it worked. clawdcursor is a free, open-source MCP server. Your AI connects to it and gets six tools to use a real Windows, macOS or Linux computer. It sees the parts of an app by name, such as "Email field" or "Confirm button", and acts on them: type into Email, press Confirm, choose High. It clicks and types by name, so a moved or resized window does not throw it off. Clicking at a screen position is the fallback. After each change it reads the result back and tells your AI one of three things: confirmed, unverified or failed. Uninterrupted workflow. When your AI needs you for a step only you can take, such as a sign-in, a 2FA code or a choice, the screen glows blue and a card says what it needs. You do that one step, and your AI carries on with the task where it left off, with nothing to redo. If you take the mouse or keyboard mid-task, it waits and then picks up again. Our own benchmarks, each run on one machine. The scope of every result is stated with it. None of it is a general claim. macOS, one machine, 2.2, 13 scored tasks per model. The whole run took 10 min 44 s for both models. The scripted reference run (the "oracle") also needs 4 screenshots: the drawing-canvas tasks have no named parts. A task's seconds include starting the agent and the model's own thinking, not only clawdcursor. Windows, one machine, 2.2. The agent never took the window you were using: foreground sampled every 50 ms, 0 steals. It made 0 screenshot calls. Details: REPORT-windows.md . Reading the screen. Windows 11, 4K display, one machine, measured 2026-10-08: text recognition of one window takes 55–85 ms, and of the whole 4K screen about 0.54 s. Waiting for a person. In a sign-up test the agent waited 4 min 43 s for the person to type a password. It made no action meanwhile, and finished on its own about 7 s after they clicked Resume. Where the app has an accessibility tree, the agent acted by name about 100% of the time. 12 of the 15 tasks stayed within their call budget. All 4 screenshots were on the two drawing-canvas tasks, which is the fewest those tasks allow. The run also found one false "ok", an action reported as done that was not:

items.title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
items.summary: To avoid the quadratic cost of dense attention over long contexts, models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 have turned natively sparse, and speculative decoding, which matters most where decoding is slowest, increasingly runs on them. Their drafters, however, still keep a context cache of their own, over the whole prompt or a sliding window. Beyond memory, such a cache costs prefill time, prefix-cache hits and decode concurrency. Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway. Both of the drafter's choices are therefore already made, and paid for, by the target: its cache and its selection. We measure how far one selection carries: made a step early, it still covers close to nine tenths of what each later token selects on DS-V4.1-Flash. We present DFly2, a block-parallel drafter that shares the target's sparsity. Each draft layer reads the KV its paired target layer cached (KV sharing), at the positions that layer's indexer selected, a fixed number anywhere in the context (Index sharing). DFly2 thus runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. On DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Hy4~flash, whose sparse attention and architecture differ, it accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe, over general, long-context and agentic benchmarks. Its margin over the stronger baseline widens from 3.9%-10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic ones. At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, its throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K sets.

items.title: Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5
items.story_key: story|ver:2.5|title:taking trainium3 to the track generating videos with ltx 2 5
items.content_excerpt: Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine ( trn3.48xlarge , 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work. With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos? I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result. I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API. For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines. The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened: Each shot has a name and a prompt , and can have a seed , to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next: Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames ( to ), and the shots after it start from its last frames ( from ). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and m

items.title: Kolpona: An Agentic Framework with Gradient-Free Neuron Programming for RTL Generation
items.summary: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) for register-transfer level (RTL) design are usually improved by fine-tuning on curated Verilog corpora, which needs large sets of verified designs and GPU training. We present Kolpona, an agentic framework that improves such models without gradient training. Its first component is neuron programming, a new form of weight-space programming (WSP) that writes single neurons in closed form into the weights to remove failure habits found on practice tasks, and keeps each edit only when testbench results on fresh tasks favour it. At inference time, tool-using agents propose designs, and a label-free selection stage delivers one design per task from the specification, the candidates and their simulations alone. On Qwen3.5-4B, edits to 16 neurons raise the VerilogEval v2 pass@1 of the model alone from 31.7% to 55.4%, and the full framework reaches 77.6%. On Qwen3.8-27B, Kolpona lifts pass@1 from 73.1% to 94.9% on VerilogEval v2 and from 66.0% to 92.0% on RTLLM v2.1 on a single 32 GB GPU, above every published system in our comparison. The RTL edits also carry over to Python and raise the pass@1 of the 4B model alone from 84.8% to 91.5% on HumanEval+ and from 67.7% to 77.5% on MBPP+.

items.title: Ten MCP Servers, Still Too Little Context | Birgitta Boeckeler
items.summary:
Context engineering starts with admitting that not all context is the same. Birgitta Boeckeler, now a principal engineer at Unblocked after almost 14 years at Thoughtworks, splits it into codified context you author and ambient context your agents pull from the environment, and explains why each needs its own delivery lifecycle.

Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks:
https://tessl.co/p7w

Recorded live at AI DevCon NYC 2026, Simon Maple sits down with Birgitta to dig into why ten MCP servers can still leave an agent with too little context, how a context engine settles a conflict between a Slack thread and a README (often by checking the code), and when ambient knowledge should be promoted into a skill. Then stay for her full DevCon talk, Context != Context: One Window, Different Lifecycles, on what it takes to ingest, evaluate, assemble and observe ambient context.

What we cover:
– Codified vs ambient context, and why they need different delivery mechanisms
– Security and permissions when agents read and post organizational context
– Why MCP servers can leave an agent with too little context
– How context conflicts get resolved: recency, the code and an expert graph
– When ambient context should become a skill, and how to evaluate a context engine
– Birgitta's AI DevCon talk: a context engineering lifecycle for ambient context

Chapters:
00:00:00 - Introduction
00:03:56 - Security and permissions in a context layer

00:16:10 - Where organizational context helps most
00:19:04 - How a context engine resolves conflicting context
00:21:32 - When ambient context should become a skill

items.title: The Agent Lake
items.summary: An agent lake holds every trace your agents produce. See how LangSmith finds high-signal traces at scale and turns them into fixes and fine-tuned models.
items.content_excerpt: The trace of an agent is the system of record of what the agent did. It contains rich information about user intent, agent trajectory, and final outcome achieved. The simplest way to use these traces is as a debugging tool to visualize the sequence of steps an LLM application took and determine what went wrong. As agent traces become longer (as agents become more powerful) and more plentiful (as agents reach production), this manual debugging no longer scales. In order to use this trace data to drive continuous improvement of agents at scale, you need two things: We’ve been working on both of these for nearly two years. The first big piece we launched was SmithDB , a purpose-built database for traces. Over the past few months, we’ve been increasing our focus on “intelligent compute”. The reason you need “intelligent compute” is that these agent traces themselves are traces of unstructured reasoning, so intelligence is required to analyze them. In traditional data engineering, a data lake stores a shared corpus of data that different engines can query and process. As we’ve built LangSmith, we’ve noticed our platform architecture converging to that as well: a shared corpus of agent data (stored in SmithDB) with many different forms of “intelligent compute” running over it. Traditional data lakes like Snowflake and Databricks don’t have storage or “intelligent compute” optimized for this agent data. As more and more of the data a company generates becomes agent traces, we think it is important to develop this new type of platform. Most of what lands in the agent lake is traces. A trace records every step of an agent run, from the user’s input through each model call and tool call to the final output, and multi-turn conversations are grouped into threads so the whole interaction can be read together. Our agent lake, LangSmith, ingests traces from billions of agent runs per month. Some customers, like Clay, send us hundreds of millions of events per day. This kind of scale is why we built SmithDB , which is the industry’s most performant database specifically for real-time workloads on top of agent trace data. The agent lake also holds outcomes. Traces show you how the agent worked; outcomes show you the impact of that work. There are two dimensions on which to think about outcomes. First is how outcomes map to threads and/or traces . Some outcomes map 1-to-1 to a thread or trace. For example, a thumbs down on a trace means that agent response for that turn was

items.title: Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference
items.story_key: model:nemotron|ver:3.5|title:building on nemotron 3 5 parse open data fine tuning and faster inference
items.content_excerpt: We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse , a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents. Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference . We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications. Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation. This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process. Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples : rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values. Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples : rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships. items.title: Interactive Proofs as a Unified Framework for Evaluating and Leveraging Verifiable Proof Generation by LLM Agents
items.summary: Recent advances in LLM-assisted theorem proving and program verification have attracted widespread attention. Beyond determining whether a proposition is true, LLM agents must produce evidence that can be independently checked by humans or formal verification tools. To evaluate the underlying, protocol-agnostic ability of LLM agents to construct verifiable proofs-rather than their proficiency with any particular proof language or verification tool, we introduce Merlin-Bench. Drawing on interactive proof systems from computational complexity theory, we cast an LLM agent as the prover: under a designated protocol, the agent interacts with a formal verifier to substantiate its claimed answer to a problem instance. We develop an automated framework for constructing test cases and use it to create 100 cases across 15 problem families, each formulated within this prover-verifier framework. Experiments with 10 frontier LLMs across multiple agent harnesses show that reliably producing verifiable proofs in accordance with specified protocols remains a substantial challenge. Our case studies further provide actionable insights into improving agents' ability to generate verifier-accepted proofs: tool use is essential for completing practical proof tasks; different forms of guidance, ranging from engineering instructions to problem-specific knowledge, substantially affect success rates on interactive-proof tasks; and proof-solving experience distilled from abstract tasks can transfer to concrete, real-world verification tasks.

items.title: Built for trust and control: Powering the next wave of AI agents across Google Workspace and Google Cloud
items.summary:
For over 20 years, we have protected 4 billion users and 13 million organizations in Workspace, and critical enterprise and government systems on Google Cloud. From personal and financial records to board materials, regulated workloads, applications, and AI models, those safeguards protect what matters most. Blocking >99.9% of spam, phishing, and malware, alongside encryption and data residency, follows one principle: your data is yours, and you should always know and decide who can access it.

That trust has powered one of the world’s largest developer ecosystems. Workspace APIs now handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, and public Google Drive API traffic alone is more than two-and-a-half times the volume of 2022. More than 18 billion reads from Drive each day come from API callers. Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed across email, documents, datasets, and cloud infrastructure, a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path. 

Today, Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI are generally available alongside Google Cloud Agent Gateway and unified protections across Workspace and Google Cloud. Builders get modern, agent-ready interfaces, and organizations get the visibility and control to adopt AI agents with confidence.

Purpose-built interfaces: Workspace MCP servers, Workspace CLI, and Cloud Agent Gateway

To help developers build reliable agents faster without forcing security teams to compromise, we are bringing agent-native interfaces to Workspace and Google Cloud:

  • Workspace MCP servers: Now generally available, dedicated remote servers for Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks. Builders get one standard interface with built-in permission and DLP checks, and native human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmations for sensitive actions. They also reject non-agent OAuth clients and work with Model Armor, Google Cloud’s prompt-injection screening service.

  • Workspace CLI: Now generally available for local agents, terminal workflows, and automation, providing structured JSON outputs and scoped OAuth sign-in across Workspace services.

  • Google Cloud Agent Gateway: A protocol-native gateway for LLM, MCP, and Agent2Agent (A2A) traffic on Google Cloud. It verifies Agent Identities against Agent Registry, enforces IAM policies and default-deny outbound rules, and screens requests with Model Armor.

Together, these interfaces give AI agents open, protocol-native paths built on standards like MCP and A2A. Permissions, confirmations, prompt screening, and audit logging happen automatically, while traditional apps continue to run on existing REST APIs.

Consistent controls across every agent workflow

Those interfaces sit on a unified security model across Workspace and Google Cloud, with core controls shipping today:

  1. Policy checks on every request: Under our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum, AI agents must use Workspace MCP servers or the Workspace CLI rather than existing REST APIs. Technical enforcement begins on February 1, 2027, giving builders time to transition. Every call is checked against your organization’s Workspace permissions, DLP rules, and classification labels. On Google Cloud, Agent Gateway enforces IAM and default-deny outbound rules at the protocol layer and routes custom checks through Service Extensions to Identity-Aware Proxy, your own policy engine, or third-party security tools.

  2. Separate agent identities and limits: Admins and users need to tell an AI agent apart from a traditional app or a person, and cap what it can do. Agents connecting to Workspace must use dedicated OAuth client IDs, paired with least-privilege scopes, time-limited approvals (coming soon), and usage quotas (billing begins on April 1, 2027). On Google Cloud, agents receive their own Agent Identity in Agent Registry with no shared or long-lived keys, bounded by IAM policies and organization, folder, and project quotas. Those identities can also carry user-delegated authorization into Workspace when accessing mail or files.

  3. People stay in charge of high-impact actions: Routine work like creating drafts or summarizing documents runs autonomously, while critical changes require a person to sign off. In Workspace, MCP servers and the CLI enforce explicit user confirmation before agents send email, change Drive sharing permissions, or make bulk edits. On Google Cloud, policy can require multi-factor authentication or human approval before reading sensitive Cloud Storage buckets, changing IAM permissions, or modifying production infrastructure.

  4. Clear visibility and revocation: A one-time consent screen is not enough when agents run continuously. Workspace administrators can view, audit, and revoke AI agents in the admin console, and users will soon be able to view agent activity and revoke access to their emails and files. On Google Cloud, Security Command Center, Agent Observability, Cloud Audit Logs, and Wiz surface unusual behavior. Revoking a Cloud Agent Identity or OAuth grant stops access immediately.

  5. Boundaries for your most sensitive data: Coming soon in Workspace, AI access restrictions extend Workspace DLP and client-side encryption protections to agents. This will allow admins and users to block agents from accessing messages in Gmail and specific files and folders in Drive. On Google Cloud, VPC Service Controls, Principal Access Boundaries, and Context-Aware Access keep sensitive data inside designated perimeters and verified devices.

  6. Strict rules on your data afterward: Our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum sets clear boundaries for AI tools using Workspace APIs. It does not allow permanent raw storage, model training, extended retention of derived data, or API scraping. Derived and user data are removed within a defined window and when a user disconnects. On Google Cloud, Sensitive Data Protection masks sensitive fields before data leaves, and customer-managed or external encryption keys let you cut off access to Cloud agent memory stores immediately.

Getting started

  • Workspace developers: Start building with the Workspace MCP and CLI configuration guide, implement user confirmations via MCP and prompt-injection protection such as Model Armor, and review the Workspace AI Tools Addendum.

  • Workspace administrators: Review connected apps and agents, configure DLP policies for your users, and monitor OAuth activity logs in the admin console.

  • Google Cloud customers: Register Agent Identities in Agent Registry, place Agent Gateway and Model Armor in front of agents and MCP servers, configure MFA or human approval for sensitive actions, and review IAM, VPC Service Controls, and quota limits.

With Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI generally available alongside Google Cloud’s agent protections, developers have an open, modern platform to build on. Organizations get the visibility and control to scale AI agents with confidence.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.330
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added sign-in to organizations managed in Anthropic's Enterprise Admin Console: after claude auth login, Claude Code applies the organization's settings and uses its cloud provider or gateway
  • Added easel, a built-in mod that draws charts when asked and under MCP metrics results, on Pro, Max and, where available, Team and Enterprise on macOS and Linux; turn automatic charts off in /config
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_FULL_SIGN_IN_LINK=1 to print the full sign-in link, if the short one shows an error or a script reads values from it
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --start-dir / SELF_HOSTED_RUNNER_START_DIR to have Claude start its work in a folder of a repository, while settings and hooks load as without it
  • Added a notice in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions when a plugin marketplace can't be fetched because its repository isn't one of the session's
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a notice when Anthropic-managed git refuses a plugin's own repository, naming the plugin and what to do
  • Added commandPrinted to claude plugin install --json results, true when the plugin's install command wrote to stderr, and commandFailed when it exited with an error, was killed or timed out
  • Added claude_code_self_hosted_runner_order_to_registered_seconds to the self-hosted runner's /metrics: seconds from work order issued to registration accepted, on orchestrator-spawned runners
  • Added claude_code_self_hosted_runner_order_to_first_session_seconds to the self-hosted runner's /metrics: seconds from work order to first session handed over, on runners started for a session
  • Fixed Claude Code freezing for up to several minutes right after compacting a very long conversation
  • Fixed WebFetch freezing the session for minutes on some pages, and returning an empty result for some others
  • Fixed ExitWorktree and the worktree exit dialog deleting a worktree that another running Claude Code session was working in
  • Fixed changes to user settings being lost when several Claude Code processes saved them at the same time
  • Fixed --continue and --resume opening an empty session or failing when the last saved message had a missing or invalid timestamp
  • Fixed the first prompt after a sleep of two minutes or more waiting three minutes on a connection that had died, on Linux and WSL
  • Fixed turns failing with "JSON schema is invalid", and session files growing by many megabytes, when many MCP tools have an input schema that the API refuses
  • Linux: Fixed Bash commands waiting seconds and showing no file diff for the rest of a session in slow repositories with large ignored folders such as node_modules
  • Windows: Fixed Bash commands running slower for the rest of a session after Git Bash took 10 to 60 seconds to start, on machines with no custom start-up files
  • Fixed /rewind sometimes restoring an older version of a file when two queued prompts, or stacked skills, ran together right after a turn that changed it
  • Fixed text and images added when approving a permission prompt being dropped when the approved command or tool then failed
  • Fixed MCP resources from claude.ai connectors and plugin servers not being attached when @-mentioned in the terminal's prompt box
  • Fixed an MCP server that subagents declare being shut down when one of them finished, while other subagents or the session were still using it
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome staying "not connected" after a brief connection problem, even though Chrome was open and signed in
  • Fixed terminal sessions on Amazon Bedrock (Mantle) started with no model selected ignoring a pinned Opus model, and still calling an unavailable default model after announcing a fallback
  • Fixed the rest of what you were typing being lost when a plan arrived in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed claude.ai connectors with different names being dropped when they share a server URL (#101856)
  • Fixed plugins going missing from the installed list when several claude plugin commands ran at the same time
  • Fixed task dependencies and metadata being lost when several task updates ran at the same time
  • Fixed incomplete backups of ~/.claude.json being kept, and displacing good ones, when the disk was full
  • Fixed a long pause in Code Mode after code that read hundreds of files in projects with path-scoped rules or Read deny rules
  • Fixed the built-in chart tool failing when Claude called it in Code Mode
  • Fixed Code Mode ignoring an MCP tool's request to end the turn from a script in auto and bypass permissions modes
  • Fixed Code Mode in auto mode dropping earlier thinking and rewriting the prompt cache when a mod added a note after a script loaded a skill
  • Fixed Code Mode not restoring a file that a script had read after Esc and /compact
  • Fixed /context undercounting system tools in Code Mode before Claude's first reply
  • Fixed a stopped background subagent sometimes not staying stopped
  • Fixed Claude still waiting for a background agent that was stopped just as it finished, in sessions run by an app or the SDK
  • Fixed background sessions sometimes waking in their previous permission mode after approving a plan
  • Remote Control: Fixed the note about background agents ended by a Stop from a phone or the web showing in the terminal as if you had typed it
  • Remote Control: Fixed the mobile apps hiding the Diff and pull request buttons, or showing a stopped session as working, after turning it on mid-conversation
  • Fixed environment variables written by a SessionStart hook being lost with claude -p --continue
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 with no message when its output went to a file on a full disk: it now prints an error and exits 1, though a full NFS export may go unnoticed
  • Fixed the system prompt keeping the earlier model's instructions when the model was changed after /context but before the first message
  • Fixed Claude sometimes replying to its commit attribution reminder and ending the turn early after the model changed mid-turn; it can still happen where managed settings set the PR attribution line
  • Fixed Esc not ending an LSP tool call that was waiting for a slow or stuck language server
  • Fixed LSP tool calls and diagnostics failing when several calls or edits arrived while a language server was still starting
  • Fixed /mcp listing plugin servers as built-in: they now stand under "Plugin MCPs", --mcp-config and built-in servers under "Other MCPs", and a server's page names its plugin
  • Fixed an "MCP server blocked by enterprise policy: easel" warning showing at every start when an MCP allowlist or denylist excludes the built-in chart tool, which stays blocked
  • Fixed /stats counting new activity in UTC days instead of your local time zone
  • Fixed /ultrareview failing or reviewing the wrong code after the shell moved into another repository: it now stops and names both folders
  • Fixed Grep reporting no matches when the pattern held a line break without multiline mode; it now reports the rejected pattern
  • Fixed Jupyter notebooks saved with a byte order mark being reported as invalid JSON by the Read and NotebookEdit tools

  • Fixed claude daemon logs never exiting inside a git repository when there is no log file
  • Fixed markdown hiding a character or two after bold or italic text when a backslash came before an emoji later in the paragraph
  • Fixed Edit refusing some valid hook commands in Claude settings files
  • Fixed Read with a page range showing both halves of a scanned two-page spread on each of its pages
  • Fixed line breaks and class stereotypes missing from Mermaid diagrams in HTML artifacts
  • Fixed the Project instructions picker in /config showing only one of its four choices in a 24-row fullscreen window

  • Fixed /install-github-app and /design-login showing a generic failure for an account on hold instead of the on-hold notice and appeal link
  • Fixed a running MCP task being reported as stopped when you move a session to the background; the background session can now follow the task, but not if its server uses stdio or sets headers
  • Fixed self-hosted runners ignoring a session until they exited, after its failure report was lost or the session was given back to the same runner
  • Fixed self-hosted sessions losing the prompt cache and earlier thinking when the list of repositories a restart couldn't prepare changed
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed tool calls behind a permission prompt vanishing with no result when a new runner took over the prompt, in sessions with telemetry off
  • Fixed resumed self-hosted runner sessions starting without their pushed work in large repositories when --push-outcome-on-release is set
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions being shown as working when Claude Code hangs at every start and --startup-timeout-min is from 2 to about 6
  • Fixed pkill -f in self-hosted runner sessions on Linux ending its own shell with exit code 144, or the runner (needs a pkill with --ignore-ancestors)
  • Fixed scheduled tasks on self-hosted runners having no tool to notify their owner when telemetry is off or a third-party provider is used
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed one slow spawn-runner hook keeping the orchestrator from claiming sessions for its free slots; it now polls every 4 to 6 seconds while a slot is free
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a 403, such as an IP allowlist's, logged as a bad secret or token: most such lines now lead with the server's reason, so update log alerts that match the old words
  • Fixed self-hosted runners' warn mode for repository settings stopping at the first finding of most kinds: it now goes on, up to 50 for a session, and says if it stops early
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed runners that start on a full disk taking sessions and failing them; they now wait for room and exit 1 after a minute with no session, unless started from a work order
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a failed start suggesting a retry when the runner's machine had no git credentials; the error now says whom to ask and what to do if the repository is wrong
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner's last_poll_age_seconds reading 0 while the runner had never polled successfully
  • Fixed the notice about a skipped scheduled task that names no organization: it now says to start Claude Code with --resume, because /resume inside a running session doesn't run the task
  • Fixed claude plugin validate wrongly warning that a mod's AbovePrompt or AbovePromptList hook never runs in VS Code
  • Fixed /design-sync deleting a file it had just uploaded when Claude Design stored that file under a changed name
  • Reverted 2.1.329's removal of the automatic retry when max_tokens exceeds a model's or gateway's limit
  • Improved the claude.ai sign-in link shown by /login, claude auth login and claude setup-token: it is now much shorter
  • Windows: Improved Grep and Glob speed by no longer starting a console host for each built-in ripgrep search on a local path
  • Improved the speed of file diffs
  • Improved /config search: most settings whose name starts with what you type come first, "effort" finds Model, and "dark" or "light" finds Theme
  • Improved /resume: sessions where you only opened a screen such as /model and left are no longer listed
  • Improved Reconnect in /mcp and /plugin: a server's page now stays open, with the cause in view, when the server still fails or needs sign-in
  • Improved the error on macOS when sandbox deny lists are too long: it now names the long lists and how to shorten them
  • Improved /plugin in fullscreen mode: the page of a plugin with errors now starts with those errors
  • Improved /ultrareview's cost confirmation on Team and Enterprise plans: it now says how much of your monthly spend limit is left when that is less than a review usually costs
  • Improved self-hosted runner sessions on Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform to say so when they start on another default model because your account refused the first
  • Windows: Improved the error when a session's folder is on a drive Claude Code can't verify: it says why, and whether retrying can help
  • Improved Code Mode: Claude is now told how to look at images and PDFs
  • Improved Code Mode: after Esc, "Interrupted" now shows under the stopped command in place of a red error

  • Changed recurring scheduled tasks and /loop to run up to 30 days instead of 7 while their session keeps running, and say when they end; tasks made before this release still end at 7 days
